newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Africa GDP to rise 4.6 pct a year up to 2000 - bank.
newsitem.headline: Africa GDP to rise 4.6 pct a year up to 2000 - bank.

text.p: African economies are expected to grow at an average annual rate of 4.6 percent in the 1996-2000 period, the African Development Bank (AfDB) says.
"If the projected growth rate is realised this will be the first sustained increase in per capita income since 1990," the bank said in its 1996 annual report released on Friday.
The Abidjan-based AfDB said improvements in external factors and deepening of policy reforms in its 53 African members were expected to push 1996 growth well above the 2.9 percent in 1995.
"However significantly higher growth rates on sustainable basis will be required to curtail the deterioration in per capita incomes and improve living standards," it said.
The annual African Development Report cautioned, however, that the projected growth rate still hinged on key factors such as domestic policies, net capital inflow and debt relief.

"It is essential that all highly indebted poor countries implementing strong adjustment programmes receive the financing and debt burden alleviation needed to enable them to grow on a sustainable basis," it said.
Africa's external debt totalled $306.2 billion in 1995.
Following are highlights of regional forecasts:
CFA FRANC ZONE STATES
The positive effects of the 1994 devaluation of the CFA franc in 14 French-speaking countries and associated policy measures are beginning to be visible.
IVORY COAST's medium-term growth will be largely driven by agriculture, although significant contributions are expected from energy and mining in the later years.
Its GDP growth is projected to average 7.0 percent between 1996 and 2000. "A double-digit growth rate might be possible if the potentials in the energy sector are fully exploited."
NIGERIA

Despite its return to market policies in 1995, further reforms will be needed to please creditors and promote sustainable growth in Nigeria. As a result of partial liberalisation of the exchange rates, imports are expected to increase, thus reducing both the trade surplus and the current account balance. Inflation is foreseen to remain in double digits. Recovery will be helped by a rebound in oil prices and continued tight fiscal policy.
SOUTHERN AFRICA
Erratic rain has dampened an upswing in Southern Africa.

ZIMBABWE's main problem for growth in the medium term will be budget deficits, unless steps are taken to cut government spending. Real GDP is projected to grow by an average annual 5.3 perecent in the forecast period. The forecast for SOUTH AFRICA is for increased private investment and strengthening of consumer and business confidence. Unemployment is expected to remain very high in the foreseeable future. Sustainable growth of 5.0 to 6.0 percent is needed to make a significant difference on jobs. Growth in 1996-2000 will average 3.4 percent.
EAST AFRICA
KENYA's economy will grow over the medium term as investor confidence builds and fiscal and monetary imbalances are rectified. GDP is expected to grow at an average 4.7 percent.
NORTH AFRICA

The region suffers political and natural problems. LIBYA is under international sanctions, EGYPT and ALGERIA face political violence, drought plagues TUNISIA and MOROCCO. MOROCCO's projected growth averages 5.4 percent during 1996-2000; TUNISIA 6.5 percent, ALGERIA 5.4 percent and EGYPT 4.7 percent.
